description: Brian and Roberta stand inside an old brownstone, gripping sledgehammers alongside a couple of workmen. She tells Charles how much they’ve missed him, how the boys are eager for his return, and that though things won’t be easy, they can work through it because they’re a family. Charles’s voice cuts in, more intense than before, telling her to stop. Roberta flinches as if struck. He tells her he wants a divorce. She stammers, confused, reminding him he said it was over with Lana. He replies that it is—then adds that it’s over between them too. Roberta stands frozen, shattered. Suddenly, two young men run across the street, darting in front of the taxi. The driver slams on the brakes, jolting Roberta forward. He looks in the mirror and says, 'Welcome to East Harlem.'

She says Roberta is beautiful, talented, and has her whole life ahead of her. Roberta asks why Charles left her if she's so beautiful and talented. name: Roberta Introduces the Spring Concert

She turns to the class and suggests a spring concert for families and the whole school. She writes in her notebook, measuring Naeem for violin size. 'If you listen to me and do exactly what I say, you're gonna sound beautiful at the concert and you're gonna be so proud of yourselves,' she tells the students. To Naeem, she says, 'Good, Naeem. Your hand's staying soft.' Then she adds, 'But if you don't listen to me, you'll sound so bad that your own parents will feel sick when they hear you. They might even throw up.' The children stare, taken aback by her words.

Roberta tells him he was present but not listening and asks if he wants people to think he’s stupid. She then has Naeem answer—the part is called the frog. Some children laugh. Roberta points to the scroll of the violin and asks what it is. Lucy snaps her fingers and says, 'The jeri curl?' The other kids laugh. Roberta chuckles despite herself.

When she tried to return to teaching, schools wouldn’t hire her because they didn’t believe a navy wife would stay long. She decided to start her own program, bought fifty violins from a Greek shop with money Charles gave her, and began teaching at a private school. Brian listens, then offers to call a woman he knows who runs an alternative public elementary school, suggesting she might have a position for Roberta. name: Roberta Asks Naeem About His Absence from Violin Class
description: Roberta walks through the school yard during pickup time, where children and parents are gathering. She sees Naeem and crosses over to him. She asks him where he was that day. Naeem tells her he can no longer be in violin class. Roberta asks why. Naeem says his mother won’t let him. Before he can say more, his mother, Mrs. Adisa, steps into view. She is a Black woman wearing a dress and a head scarf made of African fabric. She states that her son has more important things to do than learn what she calls 'dead white men's music.' Roberta responds that the class is just learning 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.' Mrs. Adisa challenges her, asking how many Black classical composers or violinists she can name. Roberta replies that it shouldn’t matter who wrote the music—Naeem enjoys playing and feels good about it. Naeem looks at his mother and pleads, 'Please, Mom? Can't I be in the class?' Mrs. Adisa places a protective arm around him and tells Roberta that she’s seen this before—that white women come in thinking they can rescue inner-city children who never asked to be rescued. She declines politely but firmly and walks away with Naeem. As they leave, Naeem glances back at Roberta, then quickly turns away. Roberta watches them go.

name: Roberta Enforces the Rules During Violin Class Orientation
description: In a noisy music room filled with fifty third through fifth graders, Roberta stands among fifty violin cases scattered on the floor. She asks the children gently not to open the cases. The students ignore her. As she pleads for attention, three girls open their cases. Roberta raises her voice slightly, asking them to stop. Two boys then open their cases as well. Roberta turns to them and asks if they heard her. Three other children begin pretending their violin cases are machine guns, making shooting sounds and pointing them at each other. Roberta tells them to put the cases down. Nearby, a boy and a girl use violin bows to fence, swatting at each other. Roberta orders them to stop and return the bows to their cases. At the same time, a girl named Lucy plucks the strings of her violin like a banjo, dancing in place. Roberta confronts her, demanding she put the instrument away. The children quiet down slightly. Roberta takes a breath and begins speaking again, but a boy starts tapping his violin case like a bongo drum. Roberta snaps, pointing at him to stand up. When he does, she tells him he will not be in her class and orders him to leave. He exits, looking stunned. The room falls silent. Roberterta looks around and asks if anyone else wants to be kicked out. A small boy named De Sean raises his hand. Roberta asks why, and he says he doesn’t want to learn the violin because it’s for wimps. She asks who told him that. He says he just knows. She asks for his name, and he replies, De Sean. She tells him he hasn’t given her a good enough reason, so he has to stay. She scans the room. No one else moves.

Guadalupe insists the others are better and that she’ll always be slow. Roberta puts the violin in its case and asks if she’s ever heard of Itzhak Perlman. When Guadalupe says no, Roberta explains that he is one of the greatest violinists in the world and that he walks with canes but still plays beautifully. Guadalupe asks if he sits down when he plays, and Roberta confirms he has to. Guadalupe wonders if he was Roberta’s student. Roberta laughs and says no, but adds that she’d tell him the same thing she’s telling Guadalupe: not to quit just because it’s hard. Guadalupe says she can’t stand strong, and Roberta tells her that standing strong doesn’t only mean using your legs—that you can stand strong on the inside too. Guadalupe nods. Roberta holds out the violin case. Guadalupe steps forward and hugs her around the waist. Roberta, surprised, gently strokes the girl’s hair. Guadalupe lets go, takes the violin, and leaves. Roberta stands still, absorbing the moment. Janet appears in the doorway and asks if she wanted to speak. Roberta says it’s okay, that it’s taken care of.
